content.intro: This lesson covers Reliability Testing and Failure Recovery. It sits in Module 24, Security, Reliability, and Production Engineering, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Reliability Testing and Failure Recovery matters when you work with unsafe invariants and external contracts. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Unsafe Rust permits a narrow set of operations whose safety obligations the compiler cannot fully prove. Every unsafe boundary needs explicit invariants, valid initialization, correct aliasing, and compatible external contracts.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Reliability Testing and Failure Recovery, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Secure production software limits trust, validates inputs at boundaries, protects configuration, monitors failure, and has a repeatable release/rollback process.

content_blocks.run_instructions: This is a deliberately small raw-pointer illustration. Keep unsafe blocks minimal and document their preconditions; do not generalize the example to arbitrary pointers.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Return the sample to its original form, run the documented command again, and compare the result. If a dependency, target, runtime, database, or hardware device is required, configure that separately before treating the result as verified.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume Reliability Testing and Failure Recovery guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

content_blocks.title: Toolchain and execution boundary
content_blocks.text: Course examples are static reference snippets, not executed inside CodeLeaf. Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
